notes: "Same Scores, Different Decisions: Evaluating JEV and Language Models for Legal Document Understanding" (arXiv 2609.27678): Jev vs nine language models on ContractNLI (123 contracts, 2,091 judgments per model), plus repeated-request stability on 30 contracts. Rows are the official-test baseline Table 1 for models that resolve to model-catalog ids; Qwen3.5-4B (74.22%, $0.053653, 86.87 s) has no catalog id and is recorded in missing[]; Qwen3.5-9B is included. The paper's conclusion: "the higher observed scores do not establish a reliable improvement for every comparator" (Luna minus Jev paired interval -0.05 to 3.11 points) and aggregate accuracy can conceal changes in individual decisions across request conditions.

claims.statement: Zhang et al.: "Jev achieves 77.38% accuracy at $0.000228 per contract." All seven hosted language-model comparators have higher accuracy point estimates, from 78.96% for Luna to 83.21% for Gemini Pro; "Flash-Lite gains 5.16 percentage points over Jev at approximately six times the cost". Paired 95% interval Flash-Lite minus Jev 3.49-6.98 points; Luna minus Jev -0.05 to 3.11. At a fixed catalog of 17 hypotheses, requesting 17 labels instead of one changes Jev median response time from 1.15 to 1.22 s (Flash-Lite 0.99 to 1.86; Luna 1.10 to 1.78): "It does not identify internal parallelism: fixed network overhead and serving policies can also affect the increase."
claims.implication: On long-document multi-hypothesis judgments Jev is cheapest and fastest but a flash-class LLM is a few points more accurate for about 6x the cost.

claims.statement: Zhang et al. stability: aggregate accuracy can stay constant while individual decisions flip when hypothesis visibility or output order changes (e.g. "Haiku changes 14 of 90 paired responses from C to D"; for Qwen4B "A and B have identical accuracy, yet nine of 90 paired responses change: four regressions, four corrections, and one switch between wrong labels").
